planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, in light shade. Hanson's lily is extremely virus-resistant and very cold-hardy, making it one of the most trouble-free of the Turk's-cap species for woodland-edge plantings.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, in light shade. Hanson's lily is extremely virus-resistant and very cold-hardy, making it one of the most trouble-free of the Turk's-cap species for woodland-edge plantings. Native to Korea, Japan, and northeastern China, it produces sturdy, erect stems clothed in neat whorls of narrow pale-green leaves, topped in early summer with racemes of up to 12 small, fragrant, bright yellow-orange, recurved flowers about 1.5 inches across, each tepal spotted purplish-brown near the base. It is a charming, long-lived choice for beds, borders, and cottage or city gardens, and makes an excellent cut flower.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil tolerant of both lime and acid conditions, in full sun to light shade. Pyrenean lily is bone hardy, long-lived, and the earliest of the European native lilies to bloom, sometimes flowering as early as late May.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil tolerant of both lime and acid conditions, in full sun to light shade. Pyrenean lily is bone hardy, long-lived, and the earliest of the European native lilies to bloom, sometimes flowering as early as late May. Native to the Pyrenees and naturalized in parts of the UK, it produces strong stems clothed in whorled, strap-like leaves, topped with 3-10 nodding, Turk's-cap-type flowers that are golden yellow to yellow-green, sometimes flushed bronze or orange, densely spotted with maroon. The musky scent is unusual and some gardeners find it unpleasant, but the early, reliable flowering and rock-hardy constitution make it a valued rock garden and border lily.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun. One of the most anciently known lilies in cultivation, described by Linnaeus in 1753 and grown since antiquity in the Mediterranean world.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun. One of the most anciently known lilies in cultivation, described by Linnaeus in 1753 and grown since antiquity in the Mediterranean world. Native to Greece, Albania, and Tuscany, it bears slender to moderately robust stems clothed in lance-shaped leaves, topped in summer with up to 12 slightly scented, intensely scarlet, strongly reflexed Turk's-cap flowers that epitomize the classical turban-shaped lily form. It is a striking, historically significant addition to a sunny border or wildflower-style planting.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in fairly heavy, lime-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade. The Caucasian lily thrives in cold northern gardens with short growing seasons and tolerates drier, sunnier conditions than most lily species.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in fairly heavy, lime-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade. The Caucasian lily thrives in cold northern gardens with short growing seasons and tolerates drier, sunnier conditions than most lily species. Native to mountain slopes at the forest's edge in the northern Caucasus, it produces lance-leaved stems bearing up to 30 large, nodding, fragrant, broadly trumpet-shaped flowers in banana yellow, flecked and spotted maroon inside, from May to July. Its lime tolerance and relative drought resistance make it an excellent choice for gardeners on alkaline or seasonally dry soils where many lilies struggle.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, mimicking the cool mountain woodland of its native Honshu habitat.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, mimicking the cool mountain woodland of its native Honshu habitat. One of Japan's most celebrated species lilies, known locally as otome-yuri (maiden lily), it is a graceful dwarf species arising from a small scaly bulb, bearing trumpet-shaped, nodding to outward-facing flowers in soft pink to rose, usually with little or no spotting. The blooms are powerfully fragrant, especially in the evening, when they attract night-flying moths. It is also notable as an ancestor species behind many modern Oriental hybrid lilies.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-5 inches deep in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the bulbs are stoloniferous, so new shoots often emerge some distance from where the bulb was originally planted. Winter wet is fatal, as the bulbs can crack if waterlogged and cold.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-5 inches deep in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the bulbs are stoloniferous, so new shoots often emerge some distance from where the bulb was originally planted. Winter wet is fatal, as the bulbs can crack if waterlogged and cold. Native to the Himalayas from Nepal and Bhutan to Yunnan, it produces striking down-facing trumpet flowers in a distinctive combination of yellow-green with a dark maroon-purple throat, up to 8 per stem, with fragrance that intensifies at night. Needs consistent moisture through the growing season but sharp winter drainage.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 5-6 inches deep in nice, humus-rich soil in light shade; this is a very late-flowering species, rarely blooming before early autumn, so a long, mild growing season improves results.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 5-6 inches deep in nice, humus-rich soil in light shade; this is a very late-flowering species, rarely blooming before early autumn, so a long, mild growing season improves results. Native to limestone slopes in open coniferous forests of the Himalayas (Nepal, Bhutan, Sikkim, India), it produces tall stems topped with enormous, outward-facing, fragrant white trumpets with a pale green or yellow throat and a faint purple wash on the reverse. It is seldom seen in cultivation owing to its late flowering season, but rewards patient growers with a dramatic, intensely fragrant late-season display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil, acidic or alkaline, in full sun; this is a wide-ranging, cold-hardy species found naturally from moist open grasslands to mountain meadows.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil, acidic or alkaline, in full sun; this is a wide-ranging, cold-hardy species found naturally from moist open grasslands to mountain meadows. Native to China, Japan, Korea, and Russia, it bears slender, erect, unbranched stems with narrow leaves, topped with small, star-shaped, upright, brilliant orange-scarlet flowers that are typically unspotted (though some natural varieties show yellow, green-streaked, or spotted forms). The flowers have a scent many gardeners find unpleasant, so it is best used in mixed plantings rather than as a cut flower.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in open, free-draining, humus-rich loamy soil, roots in shade and head in sun. Once established, it withstands drought and increases readily from stem bulblets and self-sown seed.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in open, free-draining, humus-rich loamy soil, roots in shade and head in sun. Once established, it withstands drought and increases readily from stem bulblets and self-sown seed. Native to Korea and China's Liaoning province, it produces slender stems bearing 6-8 well-spaced, pendant, red (occasionally dark red-orange or yellow in var. luteum) flowers in a raceme in early summer. The fragrance is noticeable and some gardeners find it disagreeable, but the plant's vigor and quick increase make it a useful, easy-to-grow species lily for sunny borders.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, peaty, lime-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade. This very hardy, high-latitude species thrives in cool, humid summers and benefits from leaf-litter-enriched mineral soils.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, peaty, lime-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade. This very hardy, high-latitude species thrives in cool, humid summers and benefits from leaf-litter-enriched mineral soils. Native to the Korean Peninsula and adjacent northeast Asia, it bears slender stems, sometimes bronze-flushed, topped with one to twelve small, nodding, reflexed, Turk's-cap-type flowers in pink to rose-lavender with fine darker spotting. The light, sweet fragrance is most noticeable in cool evening air, making this a charming, diminutive lily for rock gardens and meadow-style plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in consistently moist soil near streams or seasonally wet meadows in partial shade, mimicking the mountain stream-side habitat of its native San Bernardino and San Gabriel ranges. Never let the root zone dry out during the growing season.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in consistently moist soil near streams or seasonally wet meadows in partial shade, mimicking the mountain stream-side habitat of its native San Bernardino and San Gabriel ranges. Never let the root zone dry out during the growing season. A rare southwestern US and northern Mexico native found in moist mountain canyons and wet meadows between roughly 4,200 and 9,800 feet, it bears whorled leaves on tall stems topped with large, fragrant, lemon-yellow, funnel-shaped flowers marked with maroon spots in the throat. It is listed as rare and protected in several states, so garden stock should come only from nursery-propagated bulbs, never wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in open woods, chaparral margins, or recently cleared sites in partial to full sun; this species is adapted to the Cascade Range and Sierra Nevada and tolerates summer dryness once established.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in open woods, chaparral margins, or recently cleared sites in partial to full sun; this species is adapted to the Cascade Range and Sierra Nevada and tolerates summer dryness once established. Despite its name (honoring Martha Washington, not the state), it is native to California and Oregon, where it grows in chaparral and open conifer woodland, sometimes colonizing recently burned ground. It bears whorled leaves and large, fragrant white to pinkish flowers often marked with purplish spots, blooming in mid to late summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in open woodland, chaparral, or rocky slope conditions in partial to full sun; keep soil moist through winter and spring, then allow it to dry out in summer, matching this species' naturally summer-deciduous cycle in California.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in open woodland, chaparral, or rocky slope conditions in partial to full sun; keep soil moist through winter and spring, then allow it to dry out in summer, matching this species' naturally summer-deciduous cycle in California. Named for naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, it is a dramatic California native that can reach up to 8 feet tall, bearing shiny leaves in star-shaped whorls and a pyramidal cluster of large, golden-orange flowers marked with dark red to maroon spotting in June. Two rare subspecies exist (ssp. humboldtii in the Sierra foothills and ssp. ocellatum in southern California), and it attracts hummingbirds along with pollinating moths and butterflies.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this species spreads gradually via short creeping rhizomes and often leans or arches among surrounding plants for support, so underplant with low companions.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this species spreads gradually via short creeping rhizomes and often leans or arches among surrounding plants for support, so underplant with low companions. Native to the forest margins of Sichuan and Yunnan in southwestern China, it bears a loose, graceful raceme of 8-20 or more small, nodding, Turk's-cap flowers, white to cream and flushed rose-lilac at the tips, with deep crimson spotting around the throat and a light, sweet evening fragrance. Its spreading habit and shade tolerance suit it to woodland-garden plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil (tolerant of heavier soils) in full sun to partial shade; this fast-growing Japanese species can gain significant height within just a few seasons once established.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil (tolerant of heavier soils) in full sun to partial shade; this fast-growing Japanese species can gain significant height within just a few seasons once established. Native to central Honshu, Japan, it produces purplish stems bearing up to 20 recurved, down-facing, yellow flowers about 2 inches across, freckled with purplish-maroon spots and closely resembling a daintier tiger lily, blooming in early to midsummer. An adaptable, vigorous species lily for the sunny or lightly shaded border.

common_name: Black Dragon Trumpet Lily (Heirloom Aurelian Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Black Dragon is a vigorous, vintage trumpet-lily strain introduced around 1950, derived from Lilium leucanthum var. centifolium collected from Chinese cottage gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Black Dragon is a vigorous, vintage trumpet-lily strain introduced around 1950, derived from Lilium leucanthum var. centifolium collected from Chinese cottage gardens. Maroon buds open to huge, outward-facing, glistening white trumpets about 6 inches long with brilliant yellow throats, richly shaded with burgundy-maroon on the reverse of the petals. Heavily and sweetly fragrant, it blooms on sturdy, dark-red stems in midsummer, and a well-established plant can carry up to 50 flowers. A classic heirloom still offered by specialty bulb growers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 6 inches deep in well-drained soil that is not allowed to dry out, in full sun to part shade. Pink Perfection received the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its outstanding garden performance.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 6 inches deep in well-drained soil that is not allowed to dry out, in full sun to part shade. Pink Perfection received the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its outstanding garden performance. This trumpet lily bears huge, outward- to downward-facing, purplish-pink trumpet flowers 6-10 inches long with a deep carmine reverse, clustered 12-20 per stem on rigid, leafy stems. Deliciously fragrant and blooming mid to late summer, it is a dramatic choice for the back of the border, containers, and the cutting garden.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Citronella is a hardy, vigorous Asiatic strain selected at Oregon Bulb Farms from Lilium davidii var. unicolor crossed with Lilium amabile var. luteum; the Citronella Group holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun. Citronella is a hardy, vigorous Asiatic strain selected at Oregon Bulb Farms from Lilium davidii var. unicolor crossed with Lilium amabile var. luteum; the Citronella Group holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Unlike most Asiatic lilies, its lemon-yellow, dark-spotted flowers are pendant rather than upfacing, giving it an elegant, naturalistic look. A mature bulb can produce up to 20 blooms per stem in mid to late summer, and clumps multiply well over time, making it one of the best Asiatic strains for naturalizing.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this old double-flowered sport of the tiger lily is highly disease-resistant and not fussy about soil type as long as drainage is adequate.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this old double-flowered sport of the tiger lily is highly disease-resistant and not fussy about soil type as long as drainage is adequate. Flore Pleno produces fully double, outfacing, scentless flowers of bright orange densely covered with purple-black spots, each bloom carrying 24-36 tepals; mature stems can bear 20-30 flowers in mid to late summer. Like the species, it forms small black bulbils in the leaf axils that can be collected and grown on to increase stock. A long-cultivated heirloom curiosity among tiger lilies.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall for zones 6-9, or in spring after the ground thaws in colder zones, 6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade. Oriental hybrids like Starfighter prefer slightly acidic soil and benefit from afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall for zones 6-9, or in spring after the ground thaws in colder zones, 6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade. Oriental hybrids like Starfighter prefer slightly acidic soil and benefit from afternoon shade in hot climates. This widely grown Oriental hybrid produces large, outfacing, star-shaped flowers up to 10 inches across in deep magenta to crimson with a wide white petal edge and burgundy spotting, with delicately ruffled margins. The fragrance is strong, sweet, and spicy with citrusy notes, carrying well in the garden and making it a favorite for cut-flower arrangements. Blooms mid to late summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep, 12-18 inches apart, in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; plant in groups of three or more for best visual impact, as Dizzy is a strong, reliable grower that performs best en masse.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep, 12-18 inches apart, in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; plant in groups of three or more for best visual impact, as Dizzy is a strong, reliable grower that performs best en masse. This Oriental hybrid bears large, 6-8 inch, pure white flowers with bold pinkish-red to carmine stripes running through the petal centers and numerous dark red speckles. Blooming in midsummer, later than many other lilies, its sweet fragrance permeates the surrounding garden air, and the large, showy blooms make it a dependable, long-lasting performer.
